teriparatide.text: In bone-focused looksmaxxing circles teriparatide is discussed as a bone-building drug that might thicken facial bone and sharpen structure. It is studied in osteoporosis patients; effects on facial bone in healthy adults are untested and rest on speculation.

romosozumab.text: Users interested in bone-anabolic drugs mention romosozumab as another way to build bone that could in theory change facial structure. It is studied only for fracture risk in postmenopausal osteoporosis; any facial or cosmetic effect in healthy people is untested.

vitamin-k2.text: Forum users take K2 (MK-4, MK-7) in the belief that it builds bone, improves facial structure and supports height alongside calcium and D3. Trials look at bone density and arterial calcification; facial or height effects in healthy adults are anecdotal.

calcium.text: Calcium is discussed as the raw mineral for bone, often paired with D3 and K2 by people aiming at bone density, height or facial structure. Intake and bone density are well studied; appearance-specific effects such as height gain or facial change are untested.

chain: Less puffiness, better skin and physique
magnesium.text: Looksmaxxers take magnesium for sleep quality, recovery and hormone support, and some apply magnesium oil to the scalp for hair. Evidence for sleep is modest and mixed; the hair and appearance uses are based mostly on anecdote.

boron.text: Boron is taken in appearance circles in the belief that it raises free testosterone and lowers SHBG, supporting a more masculine physique, and for bone and joint health. Small human studies exist on hormones and bone; effects on appearance are untested.

bpc-157.text: BPC-157 is used by lifters who believe it speeds healing of tendons and muscles so they can keep training through injuries. Nearly all evidence is from animal studies; human data for this use are very limited.

tb-500.text: TB-500 is used, often with BPC-157, by lifters who believe it speeds recovery from muscle and tendon injuries, and some claim skin and anti-aging benefits. Evidence is preclinical, and what vendors sell under the name varies.

kpv.text: KPV is promoted as an anti-inflammatory fragment of alpha-MSH, used by people hoping for calmer skin, gut healing and soft-tissue recovery without the tanning effect of the full hormone. Evidence is preclinical; appearance effects in humans are untested.

thymosin-alpha-1.text: Thymosin alpha-1 appears in peptide-stack discussions as an immune booster, with some users claiming it improves appearance or slows visible aging. It has human research for hepatitis and infections; the appearance claim is untested.

curcumin.text: Users take curcumin to lower inflammation, ease joint soreness and exercise recovery, and reduce facial puffiness and skin redness. Trials cover joint pain and inflammation markers; the skin and appearance uses are lightly studied or anecdotal.

n-acetylcysteine.text: NAC is taken in appearance circles as an antioxidant for skin and acne, and by steroid users for liver support and recovery. It is established as a medicine for other conditions; small studies touch acne, while most other uses are anecdotal.

glycine.text: Glycine is taken because it makes up much of collagen, with users hoping for better skin, hair and nails, and for its sleep effect. Sleep studies exist; benefits for appearance from supplementing glycine itself are untested and based on reasoning.

taurine.text: Taurine is used by lifters for endurance, cramp prevention and calming after hard training, and by steroid users for general protection. Exercise studies are mixed; its link to appearance is indirect and thinly studied.

boswellia-serrata.text: In looksmaxxing circles boswellia is taken to ease joint pain and speed recovery, so users can train harder and more often in pursuit of a more muscular physique. Trials have looked at osteoarthritis pain rather than training outcomes.

bromelain.text: Bromelain is taken to reduce facial puffiness, swelling and bruising, notably after surgery or injury. Studies have examined post-surgical swelling with mixed results; use for everyday facial puffiness is anecdotal.

nmn.text: NMN is taken, and sometimes applied topically, by people hoping to slow visible aging through higher NAD+. NAD+ biochemistry is well established; visible skin rejuvenation in humans is unproven.

nicotinamide-riboside.text: Nicotinamide riboside is taken as an NAD+ booster by users aiming at slower aging and more energy, which they connect to a younger look. Human studies show it raises NAD+; effects on visible aging are untested.

chain: Slows cellular aging, lowers estrogen claimed
resveratrol.text: Resveratrol is taken for anti-aging and for a claimed aromatase-inhibiting effect that would lower estrogen, and appears in some skincare. Lifespan findings come largely from lab organisms; human evidence for appearance is insufficient.

spermidine.text: Spermidine is promoted as an autophagy-inducing longevity supplement, with some users claiming it helps hair growth and aging skin. Human data are preliminary and focus on cognition and health markers; appearance uses are largely untested.

urolithin-a.text: Urolithin A is taken by people who want better muscle function and cellular health with age, which they link to physique and a younger body. Early human trials examined muscle endurance in older adults; appearance outcomes are untested.

coenzyme-q10.text: CoQ10 is taken orally and applied topically by users aiming at younger-looking skin and more energy, and by some on statins to offset lower levels. Cosmetic evidence is limited; heart and statin-related uses are better studied.

alpha-lipoic-acid.text: ALA is used by lifters and dieters for insulin sensitivity and carb handling, and as an antioxidant for general skin health. Glucose and nerve studies exist; appearance effects are thinly studied.

fisetin.text: Fisetin is taken in longevity circles as a senolytic, with some claims of fat loss and skin protection from UV. Evidence is mostly animal and cell studies; human appearance effects are untested.

quercetin.text: Quercetin is taken as an antioxidant and, with dasatinib in research, as a senolytic, and is mentioned for puffiness and skin inflammation. Senolytic work is early; appearance-specific effects are untested.

rapamycin.text: Rapamycin is used off-label by longevity enthusiasts to slow aging, and topically in skin rejuvenation experiments. Lifespan extension is shown in animals; human longevity and cosmetic effects are unproven, and it is an immunosuppressant with known side effects.

chain: Less belly fat, possibly clearer skin
metformin.text: Metformin is used off-label by some users for belly fat, carb sensitivity, acne and anti-aging, and to manage blood sugar during hormone use. It is established for diabetes; appearance uses are lightly studied, and some report it may blunt muscle growth.

epitalon.text: Epitalon is promoted as a telomere-lengthening peptide that slows aging, which users connect to a younger appearance. Research comes mainly from one Russian group; reliable human evidence for anti-aging or appearance is lacking.

mots-c.text: MOTS-c is used in peptide stacks as an exercise mimetic that users hope will burn fat and reverse age-related decline, sometimes alongside GLP-1 drugs. Evidence is preclinical, with little human data for appearance.

ss-31.text: SS-31 is used by some peptide enthusiasts for mitochondrial support, cosmetic skin anti-aging and wound healing. It is approved only for Barth syndrome; cosmetic use is untested, and vendor products may differ from the approved drug.
